speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 7, 1983, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the Statute Law relating to Income Tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, the tax amendments in Bill C-139 are understandably of a diverse character, since taxation is no longer a simple matter of occasionally adjusting the Customs Tariff and varying the rate of excise tax.
A century ago, Gladstone recognized that budgets had, even then, become something more than a simple matter of raising revenue. "Budgets are not merely affairs of arithmetic", he observed, "but in a thousand ways go to the root of the prosperity of individuals, the relation of classes and the strength of kingdoms".
Today, taxation, or the absence of it, can profoundly affect the lives of every Canadian. Today, taxation has become one of the major tools available to Government to help shape the future. Here in Canada one need only recall the impact of a change in the manufacturers' sales tax, on the one hand, or in old age pensions on the other hand, to realize the pervasive ramifications of tax legislation. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said last year, "the tax system itself is no longer concerned with only raising revenues, but has increasingly become an important instrument in pursuing a variety of social and economic objectives of the Government. These multiple objectives contributed to the complexity of the tax system".
Since our society, including our economy, is in a permanent state of change, a permanent state of evolution, it is hardly surprising that our tax laws should be subjected to frequent review and amendment. It also follows that the rate of change in our tax system may accelerate as technological change and consumer taste alter continually what we produce and how we produce it.
The criticism has been made about the tax legislation now before us that there is too much of it, that it is too complex and that it has been too frequently altered since it was first introduced. To whatever degree there is truth in those allegations,
they are all arguments, in the end, for more frequent and detailed consultation with those who are being taxed. Ultimately, the success of any taxation depends upon the consent of those taxed. Broadly speaking, this would be more forthcoming if those paying the tax understand the process of budget formulation and are certain that their views will at least be heard, if not always accepted.
In the case of the tax measures now before us, both intensive and extensive consultations followed their introduction many months ago. Interested business groups, organized labour, consumer and various community groups have all had the opportunity to make known their objections or to offer their own proposals, both in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs and in several other forums. The result in part is the amended measures now finally before the House.
Not all of these measures have been modified, or at least modified to the degree some may have wished, but the consent of many is now embodied in the amended tax proposals upon which we shall soon vote.
How soon?

Allow me to cite two or three examples. As Members opposite are aware, there have been significant changes to the tax treatment of life insurance First proposed in November, 1981. These changes are designed to meet the concerns of life insurance agents, companies and policy holders. It should be kept in mind, for example, that policies purchased before December 2 last year are not affected by the legislation. Moreover, this legislation will exempt from taxation accumulating income from the vast majority of policies purchased on or after December 2. Regular policies paid for over 20 years or more will also be exempt from the periodic tax.
Other permanent life insurance policies may also be exempt, including those with single-premium, paid-up additions providing additional insurance on these policies. There is no dollar limit on the amount of exempt life insurance coverage which a policy holder can have. This modification was made after extensive consultation between the Government and the life insurance industry and reflects the objective of encouraging Canadians to provide protection for their families and dependants.
One could also add to the list of tax measures that have benefited from public discussion the significant tax changes for

the benefit of small business. For example, provisions for the Small Business Bond program which extends assistance to small firms in financial difficulties have been extended to the end of 1983. The program, which was to be terminated at the end of last year, reduces interest rates by almost 7 percentage points through a tax exemption to lenders.
Moreover, taxation of the work in progress of professionals has been modified to exempt, among others, physicians, dentists, lawyers, accountants and veterinarians. This legislation will allow for the lower personal income tax rates proposed in the 1981 budget for the 1982 taxation year. These rate reductions will reduce the tax of those in many income brackets and represent a total saving of approximately $1 billion annually for almost six million taxpayers.
Additionally, to aid lower and middle-income families which have only one wage earner, the federal tax reduction has been modified to $200 per taxpayer plus up to $200 for a dependent spouse. This reduction for taxpayers with dependent spouses with annual incomes up to $20,000 will mean a tax saving of $200. More than 2.5 million Canadian families will receive an additional $100 tax saving as a result of the Government's proposal to increase the value of the refundable Child Tax Credit. All these and others are examples of proposed tax changes which were modified as a result of consultation and representation.
That such changes were made should not be seen, as some have alleged, as evidence of failure on the part of the then Minister of Finance or his advisers. Rather, the modifications should be seen as a successful outcome of a process of budget consultation, however imperfect, that we increasingly need in Canada. In saying that, I do not mean that the process itself is perfect. It has been improved, but very much remains to be done. As Walter Gordon, when Minister of Finance, urged, the old established tradition according to which budgets are prepared in the Department of Finance, without consultation or discussion with other officials or outside experts, and without informing Cabinet of what is going to be proposed until a few hours before presentation to the House, is out of date and should be changed.
His immediate successor noted with equal regret, private Members of the House, and many individuals and associations outside Parliament, have expressed a desire to be given some real channel of communication on budgetary matters and that the House has also had continual difficulty with the legislative side of the budgetary process. And he added:
We have clearly not met with complete success in our attempt to balance a need for immediate implementation of fiscal measures with the requirement for proper notice to affected taxpayers without offending against the constitutional principles surrounding budget secrecy, the privileges of the House of Commons and the financial initiative of the Crown.
His successor, the third Minister of Finance in turn, noted:
What I would like is for the Minister of Finance to be able to present a tentative basis of his proposal to Parliament for discussion. The way it is now, the Minister of Finance has to present highly important advice from a very small
group of expert advisers ... and on this the Government stands or falls. I think this is wrong.
I have cited the identity of views among a number of successive Ministers of Finance. To ensure that there is nothing partisan detected in what I have quoted, I want to add the observation of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) who, when Minister of Finance, said:
I hope that it will be possible in the coming session of Parliament to examine the entire process of budget-making-
Despite this unanimity of views among successive Finance Ministers extending over two decades, we still have today the continuing practice of attempting to force modern budgetmaking into the long-outmoded practice of another and simpler age, of an age when, as I noted earlier, budget-making largely constituted the adjustment of the Customs Tariff and varying the rate of excise tax. It is as if one expected an adult to wear a child's clothing.
The difficulties arise in two areas. Donald Macdonald, when Minister of Finance, in recalling the statements of his predecessor, said:
Two aspects of the budgetary process require particular study. The first is a strict rule of secrecy that applies to the budget prior to its introduction. The second is the procedure for consideration of the budget proposals following their introduction in Parliament.
The first of these two problem areas, that of budget secrecy, arises from the need to ensure that no one employing advance information gains financial advantage for himself or herself. During the first decades of our Confederation, advance knowledge of a change in a customs tariff or an excise tax could indeed have provided an undue opportunity. But today, the growing complexity of budgets alone makes such abuse increasingly unlikely. There are today many areas of taxation where the canvassing of options, the public weighing of alternatives, could not in any conceivable circumstance provide anyone with an unwarranted opportunity to exploit for personal gain his or her advance knowledge.
What has gradually overtaken this anachronistic preoccupation with secrecy is the understandable misgiving that the consideration of proposals for tax change is not always carried out in the full knowledge of all their effects. These are areas where no small group of advisers, however skilful, can hope to identify all possible impacts of the proposed changes. Today, submissions are frequently made by groups or individuals in ignorance of what others might be suggesting and the Minister of Finance himself is limited, at least by tradition, in seeking public advice.
The basic problem facing those who formulate and implement a budget is that any pre-budget proposals are prepared in isolation. When budgets are being drafted, there is no public forum in which one proposal can be weighed against another and in which one interest group can offer its suggestions for discussion by others. For example, tax practitioners, among others, rightly believe that they can frequently offer useful suggestions for improvement in both the form and content of tax legislation.
February 14, 1983

There is another problem arising from the tradition of secrecy. As in the instance of the legislation now before us, a committee of the Canadian Tax Foundation has noted:
A complicated amendment has followed a complicated amendment and the purpose and scope of certain provisions is difficult to determine. As a matter of tradition, tax changes are usually effective from the date of the budget, but the precise language of an amendment may not be known until many months later when the legislation is finally passed.
Further, the straitjacket imposed by tradition is more restrictive today than it was even a few years ago. With the introduction of the so-called "envelope system" of Government expenditure, the need for pre-budget consultation among Departments has become yet more desirable. However, even that consultation within Government is hampered by the practice of another age.
There are several solutions to these pervasive problems. Green papers, distributed well in advance of a budget could offer various options and invite comment. Preparation of such green papers and their subsequent discussion might in turn be facilitated if a permanent advisory committee on taxation were to be created by the Department of Finance, as the Department of National Revenue has done in the case of its tax advisory committee. As an alternative, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs might be invited to hold pre-budget hearings.
As both the Canadian Tax Foundation and the Minister of Finance's green paper on consultation of 1981 have suggested, the quality of budget formulation might be substantially improved if a committee of the House were to hold hearings about a range of options placed before it by the Minister of Finance. At a time when all Parties are seeking ways to make more effective the committees of this House, here is a way in which at least one committee could play a more significant role in ensuring the adoption of better legislation. The Standing Committee could provide the opportunity for those with particular viewpoints to present them publicly and for everyone to hear those various positions scrutinized and, where possible, reconciled. This would provide wide spread public benefits, not the least of which would be the reassurance given to those who will be taxed that their representations were being heard. From that could flow consent.
The second major area of difficulty identified by Mr. Macdonald when he was Minister of Finance, and also examined in the subsequent green paper, involves the consideration of budget proposals following their introduction in Parliament. Here again, either ad hoc advisory committees of experts or the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs could play a valuable part in ensuring that certain Bills or parts of Bills are given more thorough scrutiny. Under our present procedure, tax Bills are reviewed by the House in the Committee of the Whole. Since no witnesses, no experts, are permitted in the Committee of the Whole, their contributing remains unavailable to Members. As the recent green paper concluded:

The key to more effective Parliamentary consideration of budget measures lies not so much in major reform to parliamentary procedures as in a more thorough and focused discussion at each stage, from the budget through to the passage of budget legislation. This discussion can be improved through practices such as the tabling of comprehensive notices of Ways and Means, and the provision of technical explanations. It can also be helped by the use of standing or special committees where circumstances warrant.
These cautious and even arid words mask yet a greater need in our society, the pressing need to improve consultation on economic matters among business, Government and labour. Consultation which should inform the budgetary process is important in itself. It is even more important as an expression of a wider recognition that, as public and private entrepreneurship becomes more entwined, consultation and greater understanding among business, Government and labour become an imperative for our further economic growth.
A variety of historical and other factors has contributed to the unsatisfactory situation in Canada today, where such consultation and co-ordination is so badly needed. In the past, and to a degree today, a small population spread over a vast territory has militated against effective consultation. Foreign investment of a pervasive nature has rendered it more difficult for Governments or, for that matter, labour unions to be certain that they are dealing with principals and not merely with branch managers. The existence of several levels of Government within our federal state has further complicated the consultative opportunities compared with those in a unitary state.
These and several other factors have all combined to make the desirable degree of consultation difficult to achieve. In my view, however, the real difficulty arises over the absence of a managed, continuing and formal consultation. In certain areas such consultative occasions do, happily, exist. But across the wide sweep of industry, no such continuing mechanisms are available to business, Government and labour.
In a report prepared by a Government and business task force which I chaired in 1976, we noted that a central problem was the lack of ready consultative mechanisms. Subsequently, 23 industry sector committees, each involving business, Government and labour, were created. Their recommendations were, in turn, reviewed by the cumbersomely named second-tier committee. This may strike anyone who is ardent to debate the issues themselves as a rather mechanistic approach to the question of relations among business, Government and labour, including the method of how budget preparation can be facilitated, to ensure that all those with a direct interest are given the opportunity to be heard. But it must be evident to all but the most myopic observer of the Canadian scene that a prime factor contributing to the current alienation among business, Government and labour is the absence of any process to accommodate their differences.
Our democratic system of Government is predicated on the assumption that the continuing interests of various groups in an increasingly pluralistic society can be reconciled in an

approximate national consensus. For such system to be successful, provision must be made for major interest groups to consult with both the national and provincial Governments.
In recent years, largely as an expression of opposition to wage and price controls, or at least to wage controls which limited collective bargaining, organized labour has withdrawn from even the limited consultation which did exist at the national level. Unorganized workers were not, in any event, represented. For its part, business found it difficult to designate its spokesman. This is a problem which parenthetically is understandable when one considers the divergence of interests that necessarily exist among small business, or large Canadian or foreign-controlled, resource-based or high technology businesses.
These and other considerations are all in fact arguments that, if we are going to compete successfully abroad, we must work much harder to create mutual understanding among the major players in the economy by producing the mechanisms to allow that understanding to take place.

speechtext: The rules of the Flouse provide for a ten-minute period of questions and answers at this point. Are there any Hon. Members who seek to ask questions?

Mr. Speaker, I was wondering if the Hon. Member would advise this House where he finds the rate reductions in this Bill. Could he explain to the House the imposition of the six and five program that wiped out the indexing that has been a part of our tax system for so many years, reducing the indexing this year to 6 per cent and next year to 5 per cent, no matter what inflation does; an increase in taxes effective this year, as a result of this Bill, of well over a billion dollars, and very much more than that next year as the compounding effect of the reduction in indexing this year, again compounded with next year's index reduction, takes effect in the 1983 year. Would he explain that to the House?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) made a number of points and if I do not recollect them all, I am sure he will return to his question.
His first point was the capping of indexing of income taxation, the old age pensions and Family Allowances. The Member did note that what inflation is in 1983 will determine the degree to which the capping will limit for some Canadians the increase in those programs. The Bank of Nova Scotia, for example, recently forecast, it seems with some confidence, the rate of increase in the CPI to be 6 per cent in 1983. If that is the case, there would then be no difference between the capping of income taxation of the old age pensions and Family Allowances and the actual rate of increase of the CPI.
The Hon. Member would, of course, want to keep in mind that those who are in receipt of the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the Child Tax Credit are not affected by the capping of the two programs, and are indeed compensated for the capping of Old Age Security and Family Allowances.
The Hon. Member asked about the reduction in income tax rates, if I understood him correctly. Indeed, the Bill will bring into law the lower personal income tax rates proposed in the 1981 budget for the 1982 taxation year. This reduces the tax in many income brackets and represents a total saving of about a billion dollars for an estimated 5.8 million Canadians.
I mentioned during the course of my statement the fact that the federal tax reduction has been revised to provide a flat $200 deduction per taxpayer, plus up to $200 for a dependent spouse. Therefore, we shall see substantial tax savings for Canadians, both in terms of their marginal rates and in terms of the federal tax reduction for the taxation year 1982 and beyond.

Mr. Speaker, the Member is completely off base. He knows we are not talking about old age pensions and Family Allowances. We are talking about income tax in Bill C-139. This Bill takes away indexing from the income tax system and will increase taxes this year by well over a billion dollars and next year by nearly $2 billion. Why is he talking about a tax reduction? Why does he not make some sense?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren) gave a welcome insight into possible changes in the budgetary process. This would have been fine in a budget speech, but this is an income tax Bill. I would like to know more about what the Hon. Member is thinking with regard to the income tax changes. That is what he should have been talking about this morning.
He is a businessman and no doubt a lot of his constituents seek funds for investment in their businesses. What does he think about the turning into public coffers of all those funds which are going to be collected under the changes in IAACs and forward-averaging? I trust he understands net forwardaveraging of moneys due will be paid into the Crown and then drawn back as the taxpayer requires. That places the money in the hands of the Crown. Under the IAACs, moneys were placed in the hands of trust companies or into RRSPs or an annuity contract, and were available for investment in private sources. Will the Member give us the benefit of his thinking as to whether there is preference for forward-averaging or IAACs from an industrial and commercial point of view?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises a question which is of substantial complexity and obviously has a different impact on different companies in different ways. Broadly speaking, it is fair to say that taxpayers who benefited from IAACs in the past will benefit from the reduction in the marginal rate under the new forward-averaging scheme. I

believe that the Hon. Member and I would agree that, on balance, the new system is both more equitable and lessens the opportunity for-abuse is a strong word, but distortion than under the previous system. Indeed on balance, the combination of the IAAC provision and the net averaging would be of benefit to many businesses.

The Hon. Member, perhaps unwittingly, avoided answering my question. I did not ask what benefits the individual taxpayer would have under IAAC or forwardaveraging. From a philosophical point of view, the money that is paid into these provisions will go into the public coffers as against the private coffers. That is the philosophy I would like the Hon. Member to explain to me.

Mr. Speaker, under the new legislation for lAACs, previously the money could be withheld and an annuity purchased or other private arrangements made. The basic philosophy of the Government in this instance was that this gave to those taxpayers, those investing in IAACs, an opportunity which was unavailable to others. It was a system which prevented a more equitable character in our tax system. There is some argument for this change. In seeking greater equity in the tax system, which is indeed one of the major elements of the tax legislation now before us, the new system will provide for that. I support it. I think it is a positive move.

speechtext:
The time for questions and answers has expired.
Income Tax
Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear!

That is the first time I have received applause like that!
Today I want to speak on one particular aspect of taxation, an aspect which has largely been neglected in Bill C-139. I see the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) smiling. She knows what the subject is going to be. It is going to be the question of taxation as it affects Northern Canada, Northern taxation. As a Member of Parliament for that part of the country, I receive more letters of complaint regarding taxation than letters of complaint regarding even the Post Office. Therefore, the importance of the issue to people living in the North can be seen.
The present system of taxation as it affects Northern Canada is grossly unfair and inequitable. It results in Northerners proportionately paying much greater taxes than their Southern counterparts. I will explain why this happens.
The cost of living in the North is much greater than in the South. If you look at the Government's statistics and the results of spatial surveys, you find that in the more cosmopolitan, larger areas of the North, such as Yellowknife and Whitehorse, the costs there on a raw basis exceed those in Edmonton by about 25 per cent. A little further north, say, in the Inuvik area, costs on a raw basis are again some 50 per cent greater. In all of the smaller settlements, costs can be 75 per cent or 100 per cent greater than they are is a comparable place in the South.
When one looks at these raw costs-the supermarket prices, the price of housing, electricity and so on-one finds that the costs in the North are even higher than they would appear to be from those surveys. There is a lack of alternatives in the North. In the South, if you do not want to pay the supermarket prices for eggs or strawberries, you can go out to the farms and buy them directly. You can shop around. There are a large number of secondhand stores and secondhand merchandise can be purchased. This is not the case in the North. And when you consider the cost of electricity and heating oil which are necessary to heat the houses because there is no gas or other alternatives, you find that a much greater amount of electricity is needed and a much greater quantity of oil. Also, the price of electricity might be, say, four times higher than the price in Ottawa and half as much again might be needed to heat the houses. That, of course, increases the cost of living to a great extent. Needless to say, there is greater wear and tear on vehicles because of gravel roads and the cold weather.
When you add all this up, even in the Southern parts of the North, you find the real cost of living is going to be at least 50 per cent greater than that, for instance, in Edmonton. This means, Mr. Speaker, that if you are going to enjoy the same standard of living in the North as is enjoyed in the South, more money is needed. It is that simple.

February 14, 1983
Income Tax
Looking at the difference between Edmonton, Yellowknife and Inuvik, a family living on an income of $30,000 in Edmonton would need in Yellowknife an income of $45,000, and in Inuvik an income of some $60,000, to achieve the same standard of living.
Now enters the tax system! In Canada we have a tax system which contains a rapidly progressive way of computing taxes. A person does not have to make too much money before his marginal tax rate, federal and provincial or federal and territorial, reaches 40 per cent or 50 per cent. Let us take the difference between Edmonton and Inuvik now. If an employer in Inuvik gave an employee an additional $30,000 a year to make his standard of living equivalent, and the marginal tax rate was 50 per cent, he would end up with only an additional $15,000 a year, giving him $45,000 in total. This would buy him the same standard of living as that of someone earning $22,500 a year in Edmonton.
We can see very easily, therefore, that the unfair tax system results in a lower standard of living for Northerners. Incidentally, you might say the same is true of corporate income taxes. This is, evidently, grossly unjust and the system needs radical adjustment. I will refer later in my presentation, Mr. Speaker, to what the nature of the adjustment should be.
The inherent unfairness of the Northern taxation system has given rise to another phenomenon. Because it is impossible for an employer properly to compensate an employee in cash or in wages because of the great tax bite, the system of various allowances and subsidies has evolved. People did not really want this sytem but it was thrust upon them because of the tax system which we have in Canada. In particular, the Government itself, the people involved in the Government offices in the North, did not want it, but it was thrust upon them by directives from Ottawa.
The most common allowance or benefit for people in the North has been the subsidization of housing. Either a house has been provided to an employee at less than market rent, which, of course, would be, perhaps, two or three times higher than here in Ottawa, or cash has been advanced to help subsidize the payment of rent.
Another very common benefit which employees have been granted in the North has been vacation travel assistance, one or two trips per year for each family, either to Montreal for people in the Eastern Arctic, or Edmonton for people in the Western Arctic.
This has been a very common system of encouraging people to take up employment in the North. This system worked reasonably well until about 1978. At that time the Department of National Revenue, through strict interpretation of the Income Tax Act-and under a strict interpretation these benefits and allowances are taxable-started making threatening noises. It threatened to disrupt the system which had grown up, a system to which Revenue Canada up to that time had turned a very sensible blind eye. In 1978-79 the debate raged, so to speak, and I remember it was a very important issue in election campaigns in the North in 1979 and 1980.
In the 1980 campaign, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who was then Leader of the Opposition, said that if he was elected he would look into the tax system in the North
and bring about permanent changes. But as so very often happens, especially with the Government opposite, once the election was over and the Liberal Party had been returned to office, they forgot all about the promises which had been made during the course of the election campaign. This resulted, Mr. Speaker, in a public outcry at the betrayal which had taken place.
When the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) travelled to Yellowknife and Whitehorse, he was greeted there by people with placards complaining about the broken promises and the fact that the tax system there was to be made even more unfair. This public pressure resulted in a remission order with which most Members of this House are now familiar. The taxes which should have been collected with respect to certain housing and vacation travel allowances were to be rescinded. In a way, this was unfair because the same benefit, by different names, resulted in it either being taxable or non-taxable. Also travel benefits given for medical or educational purposes were deemed to be taxable, whereas those for vacation travel were deemed to be nontaxable. This remission order lasted from year to year and was renewed annually because of the continuing public pressure. It was renewed at the time of the last budget until the end of 1983.
The year-to-year suspense has made it very difficult for proper planning to take place. It was extremely difficult for labour negotiations to take place when they did not know whether the benefits and salaries, and all the other things which were up for negotiation at the table, were to be taxable next year or not. It was very difficult for labour negotiations to take place. In any event, after two or three years of living with this remission order we kind of got used to it. We changed some of the names of the various allowances to make them fit in with the wording of the remission order.
During 1982 the committee of public servants was established here. It had members from Treasury Board, Finance, Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Mines and a number of other Departments. It had been set up to look at the issue and try to come up with some permanent and sensible solutions. Unfortunately, not one Northerner was on the committee. There was one lady who had been born at Port Radium but who had left there when she was seven years old. All these people were from Ottawa. Policies are being made which affect people from far-flung places in Canada by people who know only Ottawa. Time and again Northerners requested permission to participate in the exercise but they were denied.
The result of the committee study was announced in a press release by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on December 2, 1982 and brought about the most bureaucratic, unintelligible system that could possibly be devised by the most twisted brains in the Department of Finance. The simple
February 14, 1983

remission order was to be phased out over a period of years and was to be replaced by a complex, accountant's nightmare, containing such things as the repugnant principle of imputed rent. There was no way that the man on the street could understand what was about to hit him. Furthermore, tax accountants or tax lawyers could not compute the effect of this because regulations did not exist. All that existed was a press release from the Minister of Finance. This kind of thing is happening frequently, Mr. Speaker; we are getting Government by press release, not Government by regulation. Apparently the new system is to be implemented by a series of remission orders, not by changes to the Income Tax Act or its regulations, and so the uncertainty will continue.
The effect of the proposed system will be to drive people out of Northern Canada, including indigenous Northerners. I know a lot of people who have gone already because they can get a better deal in Southern Canada, when taxation is taken into consideration, than they can in their own area.
This move reduces industry and reduces development in the North. It puts marginal operations out of business. At Pine Point, which is suffering from low lead and zinc prices, three or four hundred people have already been laid off. If this tax threat is implemented, and I presume it will be unless there is a change of heart on the part of the Minister, it will result in another $2 or $3 million burden on the mine or on its employees. That could very well mean that the mine will never get back into production.
This measure will increase the cost of Government in the North. More people work in Government there than in anything else. It will encourage fly-in, fly-out operations. If an industry employs people who live in Edmonton and flies them in, the cost is not considered taxable; they are just going backwards and forwards to work, although the distance may be 1,000 or 1,500 miles. If people are located in the North, however, and taken out to Edmonton a few times a year for a holiday, the cost is taxable.
Not too long ago I was speaking to the chief executive officer of Echo Bay Mines. He told me that if this system is put in place, 50 people who would have been located in Yellowknife would now be located in Edmonton. About half of them would be professional and managerial people, so this provision is taking the brains out of the North and putting them in the South. Perhaps that is what the Government wants. It does not want tax revenues generated in the North to be used there as that would give rise to self-sufficiency. It would rather keep northerners dependent. It does not want people to make the North their home but wants to keep the Ottawa bureaucratic control over that part of the country.
I should like to suggest what I-and some people of all political persuasions-consider to be the real solution, Mr. Speaker. Even the few remaining Liberals in the Northwest Territories have come to the same conclusion and I am sorry that their advice has been disregarded by the Government.
Any change must be permanent and it must be made to the Income Tax Act. We cannot live from year to year with remission orders. The change must be simple and easily understood, not like the complex, five-page remission orders
Income Tax
that would be the result of the proposal made by the Minister of Finance. All that is required is one or two additional lines on the income tax form. People living in Northern Canada must be granted an additional deduction against income for the purpose of computing tax or they could be given a tax credit. I will not argue which is better as there are points on each side. A combination of these methods could even be used. It is far and away the simplest system and the one that makes the most sense.
The Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) went into the problem in detail and produced a report. I would commend that report to Hon. Members who are interested in the subject of Northern taxation. He points out that in countries such as Denmark, Russia and Australia- which in a way are similar to Canada as most of the population lives in heavily populated areas, and then there is a sparsely populated hinterland-regardless of the respective ideologies of each country, each has adopted the same approach and there is a special taxation system for remote areas.
I believe Australia is divided into three tax zones. Perhaps 90 per cent of the population lives in the first tax zone and pays tax under the normal system. Then, depending on the remoteness and the cost of living in an area, the tax system is slightly different. I believe they use tax credits. If we were to amend the Income Tax Act in this way, we would be able to phase out the special rules that govern special allowances.
In my opinion, Government revenues would increase over a period of time if we used a sensible system of taxation. People would be encouraged to live and to remain in the North, and surely we want that.
1 will not go through the few concluding remarks that I had prepared, Mr. Speaker. It was a pleasure for me to be able to speak on this most important topic today.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The rules of the House provide for a period of ten minutes for questions and answers. Are there Hon. Members rising to put questions to the Hon. Member who just spoke? If not, the Chair will recognize the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans).

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) on Bill C-139. One aspect interested me particularly, and that is the special problems of Northern residents as they relate to income tax, the extra cost burdens incurred by people in the North, and his plea for special tax treatment.
I was interested in his account of the kinds of special tax treatment provided in other countries such as Denmark, the Soviet Union and Australia and in the concept of tax zones. If he could provide additional information on the nature of those tax zones and some kind of solution to the difficulty we find ourselves in, I would be interested in that. Perhaps we should use the tax system in certain ways to subsidize or offset the high cost of living in various parts of the country. The concept

February 14, 1983
Income Tax
of tax zones might very well have some appeal and could be examined more closely.
My main purpose in speaking in the debate is to try to lay a broader framework with regard to the tax system. I have become, over the years I have been in the House and during the time I have been Chairman of the Finance Committee, extremely concerned with the tax system as it now stands and with the increased complexity which has evolved in that system over the years from the time of tax reform in the early 1970s. There are certain basic principles which should underlie any tax system, especially the principles that should underlie the income tax system. There are many options which can be taken as to the kind of income tax system which one can design for implementation in a country. But once you have developed the basic principles on which your tax system will rest, one should be very, very careful and indeed reluctant to violate them in any significant way.
Violation of the basic tenets of the income tax system leads to a situation where one group can say, "We are receiving special treatment under the tax system", and another group can then come along and say, "If that group can get special consideration under the tax system and can be treated differently from other Canadians, I think I have an equally strong argument that myself or my group should be treated differently as well". That is precisely the evolution in the taxation system which has occurred at an accelerated rate since tax reform in 1970-71.
We have seen the system modified in a great many ways to take into consideration the special needs of certain groups, the necessity or perceived necessity of stimulating certain kinds of economic activity. These changes to the tax system have resulted in a system existing today which is so complex and so difficult to understand that it has virtually lost the respect of the average Canadian taxpayer. When the Canadian taxpayer no longer understands and/or respects the system of taxation imposed upon him or her, it will lead to some very serious problems with compliance, because after all we still have a voluntary compliance system wherein people declare their income and pay tax on the basis of their own personally-prepared declaration of income and expenses. It leads to problems that have arisen most recently with regard to economic activity which takes place outside the tax system. We have the problem of the underground economy which is growing very rapidly in Canada. It certainly does not approach the extent of the problem in some other countries, notably the United States, but it is certainly growing at a much more rapid rate than any of us in the House would like to see. We have problems of that nature.
Also we have the problems of special interest which flow from my earlier comments that, as certain groups or special interests see other groups receiving special consideration under the Income Tax Act, they demand-and I am certain all Members of the House have experienced these kinds of pressures from various interest groups, whether they be business groups, charitable groups, individuals or groups of individuals-to be treated somehow separately and in a special
way under the provisions of that Act. This leads to even greater chaos, if I can use that term, in the public understanding of what is fair, how they are being taxed, on what basis they are being taxed, whether they are paying a fair share of the burden of public expenditure, whether they are paying too much or too little. This kind of situation leads the whole tax system into disrepute.
On a number of occasions in the House I have said that it is time we as a Parliament and as a people set out clearly among ourselves what precisely are the basic principles on which we will found our system of revenue-raising in the country and what are the things we will ask from that system. Essentially, income tax was brought in in the 1916-1917 range as a tax designed to raise revenues to finance our efforts in the First World War. It was not supposed to be a permanent tax; it was supposed to be a temporary one. But it became a permanent feature of our tax system, and various rationales have arisen over time as to why income tax is an appropriate vehicle for raising revenue.
The point is that income tax was a revenue-raising device. That is all it was, but over time we have seen the system become a number of other things. It is no longer just a revenue-raising device. It is a device which is now used to confer special privileges on certain groups by reducing their exposure to income tax. It is a device which is supposed to redistribute income and to stimulate economic growth and development. We are placing so many demands on the tax system that it is unable to achieve any of the objectives which have evolved for the system over time in any respectable way. It is being asked to do so many things that it is doing none of them well, and we will face very serious difficulties in the future with the particular system.
We have before us Bill C-139. I have heard Hon. Members in the House indicate that the Bill is very large; indeed it is. I have heard them indicate that the Bill should not be passed expeditiously by the House because it needs comprehensive and detailed study. I would have to remind my friends that the basic aspects of this legislation have been before the House for over a year now. It started with the November, 1981 budget and the modifications thereto. Subsequent to that budget, there were the June 28 budget, its subsequent modifications and the modifications which occurred in October. But the basic areas under discussion have been before the House for over a year. They have been the subject of an innumerable number of interventions. They have received detailed and close scrutiny by members of a special committee of the Progressive Conservative caucus, by Members of the New Democratic caucus, and certainly great scrutiny by Members of the Liberal caucus. These provisions are not ones with which we are unfamiliar or something which has been dropped on us from high with which we are supposed to deal in a short period of time.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert)
February 14, 1983

were members of the special sub-committee of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs during the month of September, at which time we received submissions, heard testimony from witnesses, prepared a draft report on the tax provisions which were available after the June 28 budget and, of course, the previous November budget, and drafted recommendations in the form of a commentary. There were no recommendations made specifically by unanimous agreement of the members of the Committee, but we drafted a report which incorporated opinions in such a way that the reader could easily deduce the opinions of the Committee as to what should be done. Indeed, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) when he brought down his October financial statement incorporated a great many of the suggestions that were implicit in the report of the Standing Committee. He made modifications to the provisions as a result to reflect those views as well as the views of hundreds and hundreds of other submissions made to the current Minister and, to the previous Minister concerning impact. He looked at how they could be modified to lessen any adverse impact and how they could be made more fair and more effective in achieving the objectives the Minister of Finance wanted.
We hear the cry that these tax provisions have to be studied in great detail. I agree they have to be studied carefully. We have to ensure that the provisions in Bill C-139 achieve the objectives which the Minister has stated he wishes. I suggest these provisions in one form or another have been under study and intense scrutiny by Members of this House of Commons for a very long time. As a result, we should be able to deal with this matter expeditiously and get it behind us so that we can turn our attention to more fundamental issues dealing with taxation, namely, the structure and fairness of it which simply cannot go without attention much longer.
In the next little while we will have to make decisions as to what the base will be of our tax system. Shall we follow the current practice, which is to use the base of income as the basis for our tax system, or will we move toward a more consumption-oriented tax base? Both methods can be handled in much the same way from a practical perspective as the current income tax system is.
We have also to take a close look at another very important aspect. How shall we apply this tax structure that we will create with regard to the timing of income? One of the big debates as a result of one of the provisions in Bill C-139 is whether or not accrued income should be taxed even though that income has not actually passed into the hands of the recipient.
Absolutely not.

I hear the Hon. Member opposite say absolutely not. That issue was carefully scrutinized by Members of the Finance Committee in September. We came up with very serious reservations about this notion of taxing accrued income
Income Tax
as opposed to taxing income when it Finally comes into the hands of the recipient for tax purposes.
The whole question of timing should not be dealt with in an ad hoc way; it should be dealt with in a consistent way. If we are going to tax income on a pure income basis, then logic would dictate that you would do it on the basis of when income is earned, not when income is realized. Our Committee, however, indicated that we probably should not be going in that direction of taxing income when earned. Rather, we should be moving toward a system of taxing income when it is realized; that is, when the person has the money in hand.
That moves us away from what is called an income-based tax system toward what is called a consumption-based tax system. People pay tax on the basis of what they are taking out of the system; in other words, a reflection of how much they are consuming in the system and not how much they are earning in the system. Also, that kind of a consumption-based income tax system leads to a much heavier emphasis on saving and investment which, of course, are the precursors of economic growth and increased standards of living.
Those kinds of questions have not been debated to any great extent in this House, and I suggest they have to be. Not only do we have to determine on which basis we are going to tax, but we must determine the timing aspect of that income.
We have to look as well at a very serious question that has evolved over the last 50 years, the question of the progressivity of the tax system. Progressivity of the tax systems means that as your income goes up you not only pay more tax but you pay more tax at a higher percentage rate. Your marginal tax rate goes up over time, which is the difference between the proportional tax system where everyone pays a flat tax of, say, 20 per cent. A flat tax means the more you make the more you pay, but the percentage you pay does not go up. This is contrary to the system we have where the percentage you pay also goes up over time. The basic argument is that this will somehow lead to redistribution of income. It means you tax the wealthier at a much higher rate and those in lower income categories pay a lower rate.
If we look at the total tax system we have in this country, from excise taxes to sales to property taxes to income taxes to capital gains taxes, as well as the special payroll taxes of UIC, Workmen's Compensation, Canada Pension Plan-which are, in any real sense, taxes-we find prior to the introduction of the income tax that essentially we had a flat tax in this country. We had a number of excise taxes, special tariffs and special duties, a flat tax system. Everyone basically paid the same percentage of income in taxation. Income tax was introduced, but over the years the progressivity of that tax became greater and the illusion was that that would redistribute income.
The problem is that a progressive tax system also has negative incentive effects. As the progressivity increases the number of exclusions, deductions, exemptions and special treatment also increase. But if we look at the tax system today, lo and behold, what do we find? With all the complexity and

all the attempts at redistributing income, we have a flat tax system again. We have gone from a flat tax system-

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) concerning the progressivity of the tax system and how we are heading toward a flat tax system despite the best efforts of this Government. Is the Hon. Member aware that, in this proposed budget for 1982-1983, for a family made up of two parents and two children and an income of $20,000 per annum, that family would have a 21 per cent increase in federal tax, added to which is the provincial portion of another 6 per cent, making a 27 per cent tax increase? This will amount to about $125 a month extra. Has the Hon. Member considered that in comparison to a person earning $50,000 whose increase in tax is only 13 per cent? What about the person receiving an income of $150,000 who has a drop of 7.6 per cent in tax? And a person earning $500,000, there is a drop in tax of 17 per cent.
Is the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre aware of this? Does he feel that is assisting in the flattening out, and eroding the effects of a progressive system which we thought we had to redistribute income? Because we have not been redistributing income; the tax system still favours the rich.

Mr. Speaker, I disagree very strongly with the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose). He will use the figures and say, for example, that tax only goes up by 13 per cent for those with a $50,000 income. In terms of dollars, that is a substantially higher contribution than that being made by others.
We must come to grips with the question of how progressive that tax system should be. My personal view, which I know my friends in the corner disagree with, is that the Government should never take more than 50 per cent of an additional dollar that is made. Why should individuals make an effort if the Government is to take two-thirds in taxes and leave them with one-third? Of course, this involves the incentive question versus the revenue-raising question and the income-redistribution question. We will have to discuss these issues logically and rationally.
Presently, the top marginal tax rate is 50 per cent and I strongly believe that that is as high as it should be. In fact, I think it should not be that high.
Come on over.

The Hon. Member opposite says come on over. I suggest to him, if he looks at developments in other countries in Liberal circles, that he will find that it is not heresy for me to say that. It is, indeed, mainline Liberalism.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) has suggested that the Bill has been thoroughly debated over the entire year. Has he looked at Clauses 121 and 122 of the Bill which were never in any budget proposals or, in fact, set out anywhere? Those Clauses specifically give the Government the right to garnishee a person's money 90 days in advance. Clause 122 provides the right for the Government to seize an individual's business without a proper court order and to operate that business as if it owns it. Those Clauses were never set out in any budget or in any manner to be studied by the committee to which the Hon. Member refers.
Under those circumstances, does the Hon. Member believe that the Bill should be rushed through the House?

Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member did not misunderstand what I said. I did not say that the Bill should be rushed through the House; I said that we should deal with the Bill expeditiously.
The Hon. Member has certainly raised a subject that was not discussed in the Finance Committee. I have heard of those provisions but I have not seen them debated to any extent. The Hon. Member is, indeed, performing his parliamentary duty by ensuring that those issues do come before the House. I would encourage him to give us his views on those particular provisions and explain why he may or may not support them.

Mr. Speaker, I am interested in this question of incentives. The argument against the public school system about 125 years ago was that poor people would not have the same incentive to educate their children. This incentive argument is of particular interest when one considers that the new tax system will raise the income tax paid by a family of four by $125 a month. How does the increase of a tax rate on families like that affect their incentives? Does the Hon. Member think that the Ian Sinclairs and the Samuel Bronfmans of Canada will have their incentives destroyed if there is a progressive tax system, even if it takes approximately 55 per cent of those million dollar a year levels?

Mr. Speaker, I know exactly what the Hon. Member is saying but the figures that he is relating to us do not relate to the income tax itself. They relate to an entire range of other kinds of taxes that he has conveniently rolled into this particular discussion of the income tax. He is rolling in many other taxes including, for example, Unemployment Insurance premiums.
No one who has to pay income tax is facing an increase in tax rates. The tax rates are cut for everyone, down to an income of $11,100 under the proposals before us. No one faces an increase in income tax rates.
There are other taxes involved. The increase in UIC premiums is required by law because that is supposed to be a pay-as-you-go system. The federal Government is not supposed to pay the entire cost of Unemployment Insurance from its general revenue. The Hon. Member is distorting the facts about the income tax when he says that certain individuals are paying
February 14, 1983

higher tax rates. No one is paying higher tax rates under this provision.
1 agree with the Hon. Member that the tax system is excessively complex. There are too many taxes that are applied arbitrarily in many cases. The income tax system must be rationalized so that we may have a more equitable tax system that can be clearly understood by individuals. If this is done, we will no longer have the confusing statistics that have been given by the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member must be aware that the federal and provincial Governments have put hundreds of millions of dollars into Northeast coal which has presently put about 2,000 workers in my riding out of work. These people also live in one-industry communities. They will be taxed on the benefits of the housing that has been provided to them.
I have brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and I have asked him to give these people the same privileges and benefits as those in the North. The Minister has not yet given me the courtesy of an answer. Will these one-industry communities that are experiencing these difficulties get the tax benefits that other communities in Northern areas receive?

As much as I would like to answer that question, 1 am sure it would be totally irrelevant to the Hon. Member's concern because I am not the Minister of Finance. I cannot make that decision. I suggest he ask the question of the Minister during Question Period.
